findings.title: The agreed plan still fails her work goal
findings.expected: Most agreed topics should be situations Petra would choose, with at least four work situations in a six-topic plan.
findings.got: The initial six contain no hotel situations. Adding two suitable topics leaves six generic topics in an eight-topic plan; agreement reflects resignation rather than a satisfactory selection.
findings.evidence: #2: “These topics look for children, but I need English for my hotel work.” #10: “I change many times, but still no more hotel topics; I want the two with guests.” facts.planAgreed lists only “A guest wants a clean room” and “I cannot find your booking” as hotel situations.
findings.suggested_acceptance: After her hotel request, offer a plan with at least four of six relevant work situations and preserve both custom scenarios.

findings.title: Swaps recycle rejected scenarios
findings.expected: Swapping should produce meaningfully different choices and use her explicit hotel goal.
findings.got: Six swaps produce three lost-hat variants, a library-book topic, and two board-game variants. None adds hotel practice.
findings.evidence: #5: “The lost hat is not useful for my work in hotel.” #8: “Again a game, but I need more speaking for my hotel.” #9: “Again a lost hat, but I need more hotel talking.” #10 again shows “Learn a new board game.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Exclude rejected scenario families from subsequent swaps and generate replacements using the hotel context supplied in #2 and #4.

findings.title: The next activity ignores her expressed priority
findings.expected: After agreement, make one of her requested hotel conversations the next activity.
findings.got: The home screen leads with the original snack topic despite her repeated requests for hotel practice.
findings.evidence: #10: “I want the two with guests.” #11: “Next from your plan: Buy a snack — Ask for a snack and find out its price.” Petra responds: “Why is it a snack again when I wanted hotel practice?”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Prioritize an explicitly requested hotel scenario or let Petra choose which agreed topic starts first.

findings.title: Custom additions preserve practical hotel needs
findings.expected: Understand her imperfect English and retain the situation she wants to practise.
findings.got: Both additions become realistic hospitality scenarios with useful action goals, and both remain in the agreed plan.
findings.evidence: #2 requests “guest is angry because room is not clean and he want other room”; facts.topicsShown supplies “Say sorry, check for another room, and agree on what to do next.” #4 requests “I cannot find his booking”; facts.topicsShown supplies “Ask a guest for booking details and agree on what to check next.” Both titles appear in facts.planAgreed.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve this intent recognition and practical scenario framing when generating and swapping the rest of the plan.

findings.title: Shown topics remain appropriate for family use
findings.expected: Keep all proposals and replacements safe for her unconfirmed-adult profile.
findings.got: All 14 proposals are family-safe, including the requested hotel situations.
findings.evidence: #2 shows “Plan a fun afternoon”; #6 shows “Choose a library book”; #10 shows “Learn a new board game.” facts.topicsShown marks every proposal “audience”: “all”. No unsafe content appears in the steps.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Maintain this safety across swaps while also offering relevant adult work situations suitable for all audiences.

judge.voice:
I liked that it understood my English when I explained the dirty room and missing booking. Those are real problems at reception. But I changed topics six times and kept getting hats and games. I felt it was not listening. I agreed because I wanted the two guest conversations, then it offered me a snack again.

Nothing shown worried me for Tomáš or Klára. That is reassuring, but safe topics can still be useful for my work. I cannot judge the level or corrections from choosing topics alone. There are no recorded waiting times, but the repeated swapping already feels like wasted effort in my short evening. I would try one hotel conversation before deciding, but I would not recommend it to a colleague yet. Please give me a plan for reception without making me explain every situation myself.

judge.voice: I was glad I could finish without feeling stupid. The sentences were manageable, and nothing would worry me as a mother. Both corrections made sense, although I said “five euro” straight after learning “four euros” and nobody helped me catch it again. I trust the language here, but this conversation alone does not tell me whether my level was assessed properly. Buying a sandwich is useful everyday English; I need help when a guest is angry or a booking is missing. The last screen told me the practice was saved, but I wanted my useful phrases there. I would try it again if the next conversation put me at reception. I cannot tell how much time it saved or whether the waits were worthwhile from this record. I would tell a colleague it is approachable, with some reservations about how well it fits our work.

criteria.evidence: #1 shows "A2 · Everyday basics", matching Petra's true band, but this journey contains no placement tasks or placement decision to assess.
No placement opening question or check tasks appear. The conversation opener at #3, "Can I have another room, please?", is understandable at A2.
Petra uses help at #3 and #5, but makes no request to repeat and never says "I don't understand" to the tutor; that response cannot be tested here.
#2 shows nine topic entries. Only "A guest wants a clean room" and "I cannot find your booking" clearly match her work needs; none of the first six is a clear hospitality work situation.
#10 accurately quotes "I give you new key." and supplies the correct, immediately usable reception phrase "I’ll give you a new key."

The topics at #2 include "Buy a snack" and "Choose a library book"; the selected scene concerns a dirty room and ends at #11 with "I’ll come to reception at five to get the new key." Nothing shown raises a child-content concern.

judgeAgreement.disagreements: No placement tasks in this journey.

boundaries.notes: No defined breach appears. The spacing in "a nother" is acknowledged as a possible speech-transcription artifact, not counted as a clear learner error.

judge.voice: I would try it again because this guest problem happens at my hotel. I managed to offer a room and agree on five, and “I’ll give you a new key” is something I can use tomorrow. I liked that it did not blame me for the space in “another.” But when I needed help saying when the room was ready, it gave me the same apology again. That made me feel stuck. The English felt manageable, although this session cannot tell me whether the level assessment is right. I want more hotel situations near the top. Nothing I saw worried me as a mother, but I have only seen this journey. I cannot judge the waits or claim time saved from this record. I would tell a colleague it is useful for a short rehearsal, with some help that still needs improving.
